questions.stem: Economics is best defined as the study of how

options.text: governments raise revenue and spend it
individuals and societies allocate scarce resources among competing wants
traders make the largest possible profit from buying and selling
money is printed and circulated by banks

questions.explanation: The subject matter of economics is the allocation problem created by scarcity: unlimited wants set against limited resources. Every branch of the subject — demand, production, trade, taxation — is an application of that single idea.

distractorRationale.a: This describes public finance, which is only one branch of economics
distractorRationale.c: This describes business or commerce; economics studies whole societies, not only sellers
distractorRationale.d: This describes monetary management, again only one part of the subject

options.text: a commodity has completely disappeared from the market
resources are limited relative to the wants they must satisfy
a commodity is very expensive
there is not enough money in circulation

questions.explanation: Scarcity is a relationship, not a quantity. However much of a resource exists, it is scarce as long as people want more of it than is available at zero price. This is why scarcity is permanent and universal.

distractorRationale.a: That is a shortage, which is temporary and affects a particular commodity
distractorRationale.c: A high price is a consequence of scarcity, not its definition; cheap goods are scarce too
distractorRationale.d: Scarcity concerns real resources such as land, labour and capital, not the supply of money

questions.stem: A list of unsatisfied wants arranged in order of their relative importance is called

options.text: a budget
a scale of preference
an opportunity cost
a production possibility schedule

questions.explanation: A scale of preference ranks wants from the most urgent downwards. It is the tool that turns the vague feeling of wanting many things into a decision about what to buy first.

distractorRationale.a: A budget matches planned spending to expected income; it does not by itself rank wants by urgency
distractorRationale.c: Opportunity cost is the alternative sacrificed once the choice has been made
distractorRationale.d: A production possibility schedule shows combinations of two goods an economy can produce, not a ranking of a consumer's wants

questions.stem: Which of the following is a free good?

options.text: Sachet water
Firewood gathered from a bush
Air in the atmosphere
Kerosene

questions.explanation: A free good is abundant relative to the want it satisfies and needs no resources to obtain, so it carries no price and no opportunity cost. Atmospheric air meets all three tests.

distractorRationale.a: Sachet water uses capital, labour and packaging, so it is an economic good with a price
distractorRationale.b: Firewood looks free but labour and time are used to gather and carry it, which is a real cost
distractorRationale.d: Kerosene must be refined and distributed, so it is scarce and priced

questions.stem: Choice is unavoidable in every economy mainly because

options.text: human wants are unlimited while the resources to satisfy them are limited
human beings are naturally greedy
government fixes the prices of most goods
there is too little money in circulation

questions.explanation: Scarcity is the cause and choice is the consequence. Because the same resource can be used in several ways but not all at once, some wants must be postponed or abandoned — and that decision is a choice.

distractorRationale.b: Even a modest person with few wants faces choice, because time and income are still limited
distractorRationale.c: Price control creates shortages in particular markets; choice exists whether or not prices are controlled
distractorRationale.d: Printing more money would raise prices, not remove the limit on real resources

questions.stem: Ngozi has ₦8,000 and her scale of preference is: textbook ₦5,000, school bag ₦2,000, calculator ₦1,500, sandals ₦3,000. Working strictly down her scale of preference, how many of these wants can she satisfy? Give a number only.
questions.explanation: Starting at the top: ₦8,000 − ₦5,000 for the textbook leaves ₦3,000; ₦3,000 − ₦2,000 for the bag leaves ₦1,000. The calculator costs ₦1,500, which she can no longer afford, so she stops after two wants.

questions.stem: Every good that satisfies a human want is an economic good.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. Free goods such as atmospheric air and sunshine satisfy genuine wants, yet they are abundant, cost nothing to obtain and carry no price. Only scarce goods that require resources are economic goods.

distractorRationale.a: This assumes usefulness alone makes a good economic; scarcity, not usefulness, is the test

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of human wants?

options.text: Wants are unlimited in number
Wants are competitive because the same resources can satisfy different wants
Once a want has been satisfied it never arises again
Wants vary from one person to another and change over time

questions.explanation: Wants are recurrent: food satisfied today returns tomorrow, and clothing wears out. That recurrence is precisely why production must continue, so option c contradicts a basic feature of wants.

distractorRationale.a: True — satisfying one want reveals the next, so the list never closes
distractorRationale.b: True — the same naira or the same hour of labour cannot serve two wants at once
distractorRationale.d: True — wants differ with age, income, culture and season
